newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fearful Zaire refugees say "World's forgotten us".
newsitem.headline: Fearful Zaire refugees say "World's forgotten us".

text.p: Frightened and exhausted Rwandan Hutu refugees limp into the eastern town of Ubundu on the Zaire River, accusing the world of abandoning them.
"The international community has forgotten us," Bernard Sengiyumva told Reuters after treking for seven days through the dense rainforest.
"We live like hunted animals fleeing predators we cannot even see because the vegetation is so thick."
The Hutus, estimated by U.N. officials to number 75,000, fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals for the genocide by Hutu hardliners of minority Tutsis there.
Uprooted from their camps in the east by Tutsi-led Zairean rebels who took up arms in October, they fled once again when the rebels neared their make-shift camp at Tingi Tingi.
They arrive with swollen feet and tales of the weak or sick left or dying along the way.
"I spent seven days travelling through the rainforest. Corpses were scattered along the way," Sengiyumva said. Those fit enough to go on had no time to bury the dead.
A spokeswoman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Corinne Perthuis, says just 1,000 sick refugees were still in Tingi Tingi when it was disbanded after the rebels arrived.
Original estimates spoke of 170,000 refugees there. U.N. officials say tens of thousands of weaker refugees were dispersed in the forest and on the road to Ubundu.
Sangiyumva says refugees plunge deeper into Zaire with each rumoured attack.

Ubunda is about 90 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani, the declared target of the rebels, which was known as Stanleyville in Belgian colonial days and is headquarters of army operations in the war zone.

A rail line between Ubundu and Kisangani bypasses a stretch of rapids and waterfalls to link two navigable stretches of the Zaire River, upstream and south from Ubundu, downstream and west from Kisangani.
The refugees say their greatest fears are not hunger but security.
Sengiyumva says his father was killed shortly after returning to Rwanda. He said Tutsis there saw all Hutus as tainted with genocide -- "Even if you have done nothing wrong all your life."
One relief official said that the refugees wanted to cross the river and head for Opala, about 125 km (80 miles) to the west on the Lomani River, which joins the Zaire River below Kisangani.
But few of the refugees have the $5 locals demand to ferry them across the river by dug-out canoe.
Medical sources, meanwhile, see a further problem ahead -- the imminent arrival of the rainy season with the death and disease it traditionally brings for those without proper food and shelter.
